name: Just war theory
summary: Just war theory holds that war is neither always permitted nor always forbidden: some uses of armed force are morally justified, and they must be limited by principles. Those principles cover when resorting to war is justified (just cause, legitimate authority, right intention, last resort, proportionality, reasonable prospect of success) and how it may be fought (discrimination between combatants and non-combatants, proportionality), with later work adding duties after war.
scope: The Western just war tradition and its modern philosophical theory, as the Stanford and Internet Encyclopedias of Philosophy and Britannica present it: Roman and biblical roots, Augustine, Aquinas, the Spanish scholastics and Grotius, and the post-1977 revival around Walzer, with its jus ad bellum, jus in bello and jus post bellum principles. It sits between realism (morality does not apply to war) and pacifism (no war is justified). Cosmopolitan and revisionist variants (Lango 2014) are within it where they keep the principles; religious just war doctrines of other traditions (Islamic, Buddhist, Asian) and the study of war as military theory are excluded unless a source ties them to this tradition.
